rashi:a1.1: Mishna. Everyone takes valuations: “valuation” [erekh] is written in the Torah portion. (A vow [neder] is “my worth is incumbent upon me,” and he is assessed like a slave sold in the market.)
rashi:a1.2: Take valuations [ma’arikhin]: if one said of someone, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” he gives that so-and-so’s valuation according to his years, since the valuation is given by the years written in the portion of valuations, and one goes by the years of those who are valuated.
rashi:a1.3: Are valuated [ne’erakhin]: if he said, “My valuation is incumbent upon me,” or if another said of him, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me.”
rashi:a1.4: Vow [nodrin]: “The worth of so-and-so is incumbent upon me.”
rashi:a1.5: Are vowed [nidarin]: “My worth is incumbent upon me,” or if another said of him, “The worth of so-and-so is incumbent upon me.”
rashi:a1.6: Women and slaves: and they pay later, when the woman is divorced or the slave is freed.
rashi:a2.1: A tumtum and a hermaphrodite vow and are vowed: since they have a worth.
rashi:a2.2: Take valuations: of others; if they said, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” they give that so-and-so’s valuation.
rashi:a2.3: But they are not valuated: if he said, “My valuation is incumbent upon me,” or if another said of them, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” he has said nothing, since they have no valuation, for it is male and female that are stated in the portion.
rashi:a4.1: Gemara. A discriminating minor on the brink of adulthood: a boy of twelve years and one day, who is close to manhood but is not a man until he shows two hairs. He is called mufla because he is examined to see whether he knows how to make a distinct declaration [lehaflot] and specify for whose sake he vowed and for whose sake he consecrated, as is taught in the chapter Yotze Dofen in tractate Nidda (45b).
rashi:a5.1: Are valuated, to add what: that is, the word “everyone” also applies to “are valuated,” since “everyone” applies to the whole mishna. What does it add?
rashi:a6.1: “A vow according to your valuation” is written: [the printed text adds in parentheses: “persons” implies.] Valuations are juxtaposed with worth, and a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils have no worth; they vow [the worth of] others, but they are not vowed, since they are worth nothing.
rashi:a7.1: Persons [nefashot]: implies anyone who is a living soul [nefesh]. All of those cases that it brings as a challenge [the tumtum, the deaf-mute and the rest] are taught explicitly in the mishna.
rashi:a10.1: He teaches and then explains: and the same is true for the others; he could have taken any one of them, but he took one of the two or three. Another version: he took this one because Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree about it in this chapter (below, 5a). One who valuates a child less than a month old: Rabbi Meir says he gives its worth, since a person knows that there is no valuation for one less than a month old, and he resolved to mean its worth; and the Rabbis say he has said nothing. That is why the mishna stated it anonymously at the start, to teach us from the extra wording of the mishna that even according to the Rabbis, where he said “His worth is incumbent upon me,” the child has a worth and he gives its worth. From the mouth of our teacher.
rashi:a11.1: An heir: a person whose father set aside an offering and did not manage to sacrifice it before he died.
rashi:a14.1: His offering: with regard to placing hands, “his offering” is written three times, concerning peace offerings in Leviticus, and Rabbi Yehuda expounds one of them: “his offering,” and not his father’s offering.
rashi:a14.2: The initial stage of consecration: substitution, which is the start of this animal’s sanctity.
rashi:a14.3: The final stage of consecration: placing hands, which is close to the slaughter.
rashi:a16.1: All partners in an offering: five who brought one offering in partnership all must place hands on it, and one does not place hands for them all.
rashi:a17.1: He does not hold this: for he holds that one places hands on behalf of them all, and it is not like placing hands on another’s offering, since he has a share in it.
tosafot:a1.1: Mishna. Everyone takes valuations: in Nazir (2a) and in Nedarim (2a) the mishna mentions substitute terms [kinuyim], so as not to mention the Name of Heaven in vain, as is explained there. Here the tanna was not concerned about mentioning [the terms themselves], since people did not mention the Name of Heaven with valuations. “Valuation” is written in the portion; vows are “my worth is incumbent upon me,” and he is assessed like a slave sold in the market.
tosafot:a1.2: Take valuations: if one said of someone in the market, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me” (or if he said, “The valuation of that so-and-so is incumbent upon me”), he gives according to the years written in the portion of shekels [Rashi reads: “the portion of valuations”], and one goes by his years.
tosafot:a1.3: Are valuated: if he said, “My valuation is incumbent upon me,” or if another said [of him], “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me.”
tosafot:a1.4: Women and slaves: they pay later, when the woman is divorced or the slave is freed; so Rashi explained. Alternatively, for example where [property] was given to them on condition that the master or the husband has no rights in it. And even if they have nothing, [the debt] is placed upon them immediately, as is taught in the Tosefta: Women and slaves vow and are vowed; if they have [the means] at this time, one collects from them, and if not, one [writes a deed] against them and collects later. And a slave, although with regard to mitzvot he has the status of a woman, is valuated according to the valuation of a male, for no tanna ever let slip that he is valuated like a woman.
tosafot:a2.1: A tumtum and a hermaphrodite vow and are vowed: since they have a worth. And they take valuations of others: if they said, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” they give that so-and-so’s valuation. But they are not valuated: if one said of them, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” he has said nothing, since male and female are what is stated in the portion. This is Rashi’s wording.
tosafot:a3.1: A deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor: this implies that a deaf-mute has a worth. And as for what is said in the chapter HaḤovel (Bava Kamma 85b), “If he deafened him, he gives him his entire worth” [as though he were now worth nothing], that refers to a deafness that cannot be healed. Alternatively, Rabbeinu Tam explained that one deafened by Heaven has a worth.
tosafot:a4.1: A discriminating minor on the brink of adulthood: a boy of twelve years and one day, who is close to manhood but is not a man until thirteen years and one day. He is called mufla because he is examined to see whether he knows how to make a distinct declaration [lehaflot] and specify for whose sake he vowed and for whose sake he consecrated, as is taught in the chapter Yotze Dofen (Nidda 45b).
tosafot:a5.1: Are valuated, to add what: that is, the word “everyone” also applies to “are valuated,” since “everyone” applies to the whole mishna; this is what it means.
tosafot:a5.2: To add a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils: this implies that it applies also to the slaves of our mishna. One may ask: we raise a dilemma in the chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 42b) about a slave whom his master sold, with regard to a fine: what is the law? Evidently even [such] a slave has a worth. One may answer that here it is speaking of one who is a tereifa [with a mortal injury]. And if you say: then one who kills him should be liable, since he is included by “persons,” which shows that he is called a “person” [nefesh]; for it is for this reason that one who kills a day-old infant is included, in the chapter Yotze Dofen (Nidda 44b), even though it might be a non-viable birth — one may answer that there, in Torat Kohanim, we establish it as a case where its months were completed, and likewise we establish it there according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says that any [infant] that did not survive [thirty days may be non-viable].
tosafot:a6.1: A vow according to your valuation, persons: this implies that valuations are juxtaposed with worth. A repulsive man and one afflicted with boils have no worth; they vow [the worth of] others, but they are not vowed, since they are worth nothing.
tosafot:a6.2: Anyone who is included in assessments is included in valuations: not precisely, since there are a palm tree and land [which have a worth but no valuation]; rather, it means any person who is included in assessments.
tosafot:a14.1: His offering: with regard to placing hands, “his offering” is written three times in Leviticus, and Rabbi Yehuda expounds one of them: “his offering,” and not his father’s offering. That is Rashi’s wording, but in his sharpness he did not look closely, since there are only two there. Perhaps he counts “on its head,” which is written there, like “his offering.” Alternatively, he expounds it from the other instances of “his offering.”
tosafot:a14.2: The initial stage of consecration: substitution, which is the start of this animal’s sanctity; the final stage of consecration: placing hands, which is close to the slaughter. This is Rashi’s wording. And when substitution is called “the final stage of consecration” in the chapter HaZahav (Bava Metzia 54b), that is relative to the first offering. And if you say: let us derive slaughter from placing hands as well, so that an heir may not slaughter — that is not so, for even one’s agent is not excluded from slaughtering.
tosafot:a16.1: His offering, and not another’s offering: and if you say: since we say at the end of the chapter Shtei Middot (Menaḥot 93b), “And he shall place his hand” — and not the hand of his agent — all the more so not the hand of another; if so, why do I need “his offering”? One may answer: were it not for “his offering,” I would have said that “his hand” comes to exclude another, but his agent may place hands. And if you say: let us derive from here, for the whole Torah, that a person’s agent is not like himself; why then is it derived in the second chapter of Kiddushin (41b) that he is like himself? One may answer: because placing hands, the yevama and the heifer whose neck is broken are three verses that come as one. Of the yevama it is written (Deuteronomy 25), “and they shall call him” — they, and not their agent; and likewise of the heifer whose neck is broken, “and they shall measure” — and not their agent. And if you say: let us derive from them that everywhere else a person’s agent is like himself, since it was necessary to exclude these — one may answer: were it not for the verses in Kiddushin that teach us that a person’s agent is like himself, we would have used these three verses, of placing hands, the yevama and the heifer, for some other exposition.
tosafot:a16.2: All partners in an offering: five who brought one offering in partnership all must place hands on it, and one does not place hands on behalf of them all.
tosafot:a17.1: He does not hold this: for he holds that one places hands on behalf of them all, and it is not like placing hands on another’s offering, since he has a share in it. This is Rashi’s wording. And so it is implied in the chapter Shtei Middot (Menaḥot 94a): “Just as waving, which was extended to those who slaughter, was limited among partners, is it not logical that placing hands, which was not extended to those who slaughter, should be limited among partners? The verse states ‘his offering,’ to include them all.” Evidently, according to the one who does not expound “his offering,” he derives it from waving, and we learned there: one person waves for them all.
gershom:a1.1: Everyone takes valuations: whether for themselves or for others, for example “My valuation is incumbent upon me” or “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” and he is obligated in his valuation according to his years.
gershom:a2.1: And are valuated: a person may say of him, “The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” and the valuation takes effect, and the one who made the pledge must give his valuation.
gershom:a3.1: Vow: one may say, “My worth is incumbent upon me” or “The worth of so-and-so is incumbent upon me.”
gershom:a4.1: And are vowed: one who vows and says, “The worth of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,” has no fixed sum; rather, he is assessed like a slave sold in the market, and one gives his worth.
gershom:a5.1: And they do not take valuations: because they lack understanding, for we require a person who knows how to declare distinctly for whom he is pledging a valuation or making a vow.
gershom:a6.1: Gemara. To add a discriminating minor on the brink of adulthood: [that is,] a boy of twelve or a girl of eleven, who are close to [obligation in] mitzvot, and their vows are examined. If he is discriminating and knows for whose sake he vows or pledges a valuation, it is a vow. But before this age, even if he is discriminating, it is not a vow, since he is considered a minor; and after this age, even if he is not discriminating, his vow is a vow.
gershom:a7.1: And a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils: who have no worth, since no one wants to buy them.
gershom:a8.1: It teaches us: “According to your valuation, persons”: that even a person of the slightest worth, like these who are not valued, is valuated.
gershom:a9.1: Vow, to add what: [that is,] if it is to add the discriminating minor, we already learned that from the “everyone” of “are valuated.” Rather, the “everyone” was not needed for “vow” except because of the “everyone” of “are vowed,” for “everyone” applies to all of them: to “are valuated,” to “vow” and to “are vowed.”
gershom:a10.1: Rather, to add one less than a month old, who is vowed [i.e., his assessment may be pledged]. And although it is taught explicitly in the mishna, he teaches and then explains in the mishna, since he derives it from “everyone.” And if you say, what is different [about this case]? [An editor’s note: it seems it should read: why does it say “he teaches and then explains” only about this one, when he could have said it about the others too?] He could have said “he teaches and then explains” about the tumtum, the deaf-mute and the gentile as well. One may answer: indeed so; but since “a month old” is written in the Torah, it includes one less than a month old, who, although he is neither valuated nor takes valuations, is vowed.
gershom:a11.1: Everyone places hands: it now seeks to expound every “everyone” as an inclusion.
gershom:a12.1: An heir places hands and substitutes: if his father consecrated an offering and died before placing hands on it, the heir places hands on his father’s offering.
gershom:a13.1: And an heir can substitute for his father’s offering. “His offering”: “and he shall place his hand on his offering,” and not on the head of his father’s offering.
gershom:a14.1: And he derives the initial stage of consecration: that is substitution, for he now makes this substitute consecrated.
gershom:a15.1: From the final stage of consecration: that is placing hands, which is immediately followed by slaughter, and the consecration comes to its end. And just as an heir is excluded from placing hands, so too from substitution.
gershom:a16.1: Hamer yamir: [“hamer”] is an inclusion, since it would have sufficed to say “if he shall substitute” [im yamir]. And they derive the final stage of consecration from the initial stage: they derive placing hands from substitution.
gershom:a17.1: His offering, and not the offering of a gentile, etc.: “his offering” is written three times concerning placing hands with peace offerings. “His offering,” and not the offering of a gentile, since a gentile’s offering does not require placing hands; “his offering,” and not the offering of another, since a person does not place hands on an offering that is not his; “his offering,” to include all the owners of the offering in placing hands.
gershom:a18.1: [An editor’s note: this should read “And according to Rabbi Yehuda it does not come for this, but to include a woman,” and it belongs above, before the comment beginning “And they derive.” — And according to Rabbi Yehuda, so; not to include a woman.] To include all the owners of an offering in placing hands: if two or three partners share an offering, they all place hands on it. A gentile and another are derived from one verse, that is, [an offering] that is not his.
rashi:b1.1: A gentile and another: that an Israelite does not place hands on a gentile’s offering, nor on the offering of another Israelite.
rashi:b1.2: Are derived from one verse: since these are not “his offering.” But for his father a verse was needed, since it might have entered your mind that it is called “his offering,” since he is the heir.
rashi:b2.1: Since the entire matter: of substitution.
rashi:b2.2: What do we ultimately: from where do we ultimately include a woman (with her offering), so that if she substituted for her offering it would be a substitute?
rashi:b4.1: Who does not need his mother: explained in tractate Sukka (28b): one who wakes from his sleep and does not call out “Mother!”
rashi:b8.1: One who is half-slave, etc.: but a full slave is exempt, as it is written, “before the Master, the Lord” (Exodus 34:23): one who has no master but Him.
rashi:b9.1: And according to Ravina, who said, etc.: in the first chapter of Ḥagiga (4a). He derives it from the latter clause of the mishna there, which teaches: “and slaves who are not freed.”
rashi:b9.2: Lame: he is exempt from appearance, since “regalim” is written [“three times,” literally “three feet”], excluding those with wooden legs.
rashi:b10.1: This works out well according to the one who says: in the first chapter of Ḥagiga (9a), about what is taught there, “he celebrates throughout the Festival”: because all seven days rectify one another, the second for the first and the third for the second. Evidently each day counts on its own, since each has a make-up, and one can say that one who was not fit on the first day but was fit on the second is obligated.
rashi:b10.2: Rectify the first: one who was fit and obligated to sacrifice on the first day and did not sacrifice may sacrifice during all seven; but one who was not [fit to] appear on the first day is no longer obligated, since they are all only a make-up for the first. What can one say?
rashi:b12.1: Yir’eh, yera’eh: it is written yir’eh [“he shall see”], and we read yera’eh [“he shall appear”]. Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to see you, and He is whole in both eyes, so one comes to appear: that He be seen by you with both your eyes.
rashi:b13.1: In the initial mishna: before Beit Hillel conceded, he had the presumptive status of a slave. But after they changed their view and conceded, since it is in our power to free him, he is considered as freed, since his master has no authority over him, and “another master” does not apply to him.
rashi:b17.1: Who reached the age of training: this is a dispute in the last chapter of Yoma (82a). One says: from eight, from nine [the printed text reads six and seven, corrected in brackets to eight and nine]; and one says: from nine, from ten, when one trains him [to fast] for some hours.
tosafot:b1.1: A gentile and another are derived from one verse: since an Israelite does not place hands on a gentile’s offering nor on another’s offering, they are derived from one verse, as these are not “his offering.” But for his father a verse was needed, since it might have entered your mind… [several words here are bracketed as doubtful in the printed text]. Just as the priest sacrifices an offering that is not his, it might have entered your mind that an Israelite places hands on another’s offering; and for a gentile’s offering too, it might have entered your mind that [a priest] places hands, just as the libations for it are given from public funds, as is said in the first chapter of Temura (2b). That is why “his offering” comes, to exclude both of them, since in any event it is not his.
tosafot:b2.1: To include a woman: so that if she substituted for her offering it is a substitute; this is Rashi’s wording. Since the entire matter speaks only in the masculine, etc.: and although the whole Torah was also stated in the masculine, nevertheless we say that a woman is juxtaposed to a man for all punishments; but with regard to substitution, were it not for the verse she would not be equal to a man, as explained there, in the first chapter of Temura.
tosafot:b3.1: And Rabbi Yehuda does not expound “and if”: that is, he does not expound the letter vav, as is explained in the first chapter of Temura.
tosafot:b4.1: Who does not need his mother: explained in tractate Sukka (28b): anyone who wakes from his sleep and does not call out “Mother!” This is Rashi’s wording.
tosafot:b6.1: Everyone is obligated in ritual fringes: if they have a garment; but if one cannot buy a garment, they are not obligated, neither according to the one who says it is an obligation of the garment nor according to the one who says it is an obligation of the person (Menaḥot 41a), for the only difference between them is a garment kept in a chest. And as for the angel who said to Rav Ketina, “A linen sheet in summer and a cloak in winter — what will become of ritual fringes?” — that is, are you seeking pretexts to exempt yourself from ritual fringes, as explained there — and when he said to him, “Do you punish for [neglecting] a positive mitzva?” the angel answered, “At a time of wrath we punish”: that applied only in those days, when all garments had four corners, so there was punishment for one who changed his garment to exempt himself. But nowadays, when most garments are exempt, there is no punishment for one who does not buy [a garment with] four corners.
tosafot:b6.2: Who knows how to wrap himself: because it is said in Mo’ed Katan (24a), “Any wrapping that is not like the wrapping of the Ishmaelites is not a wrapping,” for they wrap their garment up to the mustache, as explained in the Midrash. And I found in a silluk [liturgical poem] composed by Rabbi Yosef Tov Elem that one places one fringe in front and one behind on the right, and likewise on the left.
tosafot:b6.3: Who knows how to wrap himself: and if you say: according to the one who says it is an obligation of the garment, even if he does not know how [to wrap himself] he should be obligated if he has a garment — one may answer that in any event a garment kept in a chest is obligated only for those who are obligated and know how to wrap themselves. And Halakhot Gedolot ruled that we hold (Menaḥot, there) that ritual fringes are an obligation of the person, since we bless “to wrap ourselves in ritual fringes”; for that is how it is inferred [in the second chapter of Shabbat, 25b, and there] that we hold [so].
tosafot:b7.1: His father purchases phylacteries for him: with ritual fringes it does not use the expression “purchases,” since presumably he has a garment; and with lulav too he can fulfill the obligation with his father’s lulav. Alternatively, because phylacteries are expensive, the term “purchase” fits them.
tosafot:b8.1: Everyone is obligated in appearance: Rashi explained in tractate Ḥagiga (2a): obligated to appear in the Temple courtyard. But in the Jerusalem Talmud they say about this: “This applies to [appearance] with an offering; but as for appearing in the courtyard, even small children are obligated, as it is written: ‘Assemble the people, the men and the women and the little ones.’” But that is only a mere support from the verse, for certainly [appearance] is not like the Assembly [hakhel], since there [in Ḥagiga] women are excluded by “your males.” Rather, it certainly appears that [the mishna] speaks of appearance with an offering as well, for we learned there shortly after: “The appearance offering is two silver ma’a.”
tosafot:b8.2: One who is half-slave: but a full slave is exempt, as it is written, “before the Master, the Lord” — one who has no master but Him. This is Rashi’s wording, and so we conclude. And although the latter clause of the mishna [in Ḥagiga] teaches “except for women and slaves who are not freed,” and we explain there that it means not entirely freed, i.e., half-freed, one must say that the first clause of the mishna follows the ultimate version of the mishna, when Beit Hillel retracted to rule in accordance with Beit Shammai. We find the same in the first chapter of Eruvin (6b) and in the chapter Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 43b): “The halakha always follows Beit Hillel, and one who wishes to act in accordance with Beit Shammai may do so,” and we establish the first clause as after the Divine Voice and the latter clause as before the Divine Voice.
tosafot:b9.1: And according to Ravina, who said, etc.: in the first chapter of Ḥagiga (4a). He derives it from the latter clause of the mishna there, which teaches “slaves who are not freed.” And a lame person is exempt from appearance, since “regalim” is written, excluding those with wooden legs.
tosafot:b10.1: This works out well according to the one who says: in the first chapter of Ḥagiga (9a), where it is taught that one celebrates throughout the Festival, because all seven days rectify one another, the second for the first and the third for the second. Evidently each day counts on its own, since each has a make-up, and one can say that one who was not fit on the first day but was fit on the second is obligated.
tosafot:b10.2: Rectify the first: one who was fit and obligated to sacrifice on the first day may go on sacrificing during all seven; but one who was not [fit to] appear on the first day is no longer obligated, since they are all only a make-up for the first. What can one say?
tosafot:b13.1: In the initial mishna: before Beit Hillel conceded, he had the presumptive status of a slave; but after they changed their view and conceded, since it is in our power to free him, he is considered as freed, since his master has no authority over him, and “another master” does not apply to him. This is Rashi’s wording. And as for the dilemma (Gittin 42b) about one awaiting a bill of emancipation with regard to a fine — or perhaps, since he is awaiting a bill of emancipation, he is called one who has a master — one can distinguish: with regard to going up for the Festival, he is not his master, since he cannot stop him from going up for the Festival in order to do his work; but nevertheless he is called his master.
tosafot:b17.1: Who reached the age of training: this is a dispute in the eighth chapter of Yoma (82a): one says from [six], [and one says] from eight; and some say from nine, from ten, when one trains him in mitzvot. This is Rashi’s wording. But it is not correct, for there it speaks of training a minor to fast; but in other mitzvot, each according to its own manner, as we found above with lulav, sukka and phylacteries.
tosafot:b17.2: One need not prevent minors from sounding: in the fourth chapter of Rosh HaShana (33a) the Gemara asks: since it teaches “one need not prevent,” it follows that we do not tell them ab initio, “Go and sound,” and then it teaches, “but one busies oneself with them so that they learn, even on Shabbat.” It answers: here it speaks of a minor who reached the age of training, there of a minor who did not; that is, with a minor who reached the age of training, one busies oneself with him. And if you say: it is obvious that one need not prevent them, according to the one who says in the chapter Ḥeresh in Yevamot (114a) that if a minor eats carcasses the court is not commanded to stop him — one may answer: for example, where he reached the age of training for keeping Shabbat but not the age of training for sounding the shofar, and so it is something of a novelty.
gershom:b1.1: Speaks only in the masculine: as it is written, “He shall not exchange it nor substitute it.”
gershom:b2.1: What do we ultimately, to include a woman: that is, from where do we ultimately [have a source] to include a woman, so that she effects substitution? The verse states: “hamer yamir.”
gershom:b3.1: And the Rabbis include a woman from the vav of “and if.”
gershom:b4.1: To preserve phylacteries: as they are meant to be kept.
gershom:b5.1: This works out well according to the one who says they all rectify one another: regarding what we learned, “One who did not celebrate on the first Festival day celebrates throughout the Festival and on the last Festival day.” Two Amoraim disagree there. One says they all rectify one another, since they are all days of obligation: although he was not fit on the first, he was fit on the second, and the second too is a day of obligation, for if he did not do so on the second he must make it up on the other days. The other says they are all a make-up for the first: one who was fit on the first and did not do so makes it up on the other days, but if he was not fit on the first, even though he was fit on the other days, he is not obligated.
gershom:b6.1: As it is stated, yir’eh, yera’eh: it is written yir’eh, and we read yera’eh. Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, who comes to see the pilgrims, [sees] with two eyes [may His remembrance be praised forever and ever], so too those who come to be seen should see with two eyes.
gershom:b7.1: And some say, from here: “And Abraham called the name of that place ‘The Lord will see,’ as it is said to this day, ‘On the mount of the Lord He shall be seen’” (Genesis 22:14). That is, He sees the place and those who come there, and He is seen by those who come there.
gershom:b8.1: Just as to see, etc.: and some say: just as seeing is with two eyes — that is, [a priest] who is blind in one of his eyes, who does not examine the marks of leprosy, as it is written, “wherever the priest’s eyes look” — so too one who comes to be seen [must come] with two eyes.
gershom:b9.1: In accordance with the initial mishna: according to Beit Hillel, he is exempt from appearance.
gershom:b10.1: In accordance with the ultimate mishna: when Beit Hillel retracted to rule in accordance with Beit Shammai, he is obligated in appearance. And although he is not yet free, since he will ultimately be free, he is obligated in appearance.
gershom:b11.1: Who reached the age of training: who is obligated in sounding the shofar, like the training mentioned in [the chapter] Yom HaKippurim (82a).
gershom:b12.1: Everyone is obligated in the Megilla, and everyone is fit to read it: for anyone who is obligated in a matter can discharge the obligation of the public.
